newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr suffers as yen surges, gold sinks.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr suffers as yen surges, gold sinks.

text.p: The Australian dollar extended offshore losses to end 2/3 cent poorer Monday as a surge in the yen and a slide in gold clobbered sentiment from two directions. Traders reported heavy selling of AUD/yen out of Tokyo as US$/yen went into a spin over disturbing Japanese trade data, which drove the local unit to its lowest level since August last year. Japanese investors were also seen bailing out of gold, which saw spot prices sink US$6.0 in hectic trade and threatened to have knock-on effects in other Australian commodity exports.
Add to that the constant fear of a domestic rate cut, and dealers could find few reasons to hold the A$ just now.
By 4.45 pm (0645 GMT) the local dollar was laid out at US$0.7440/45 having been slapped down from US$0.7519/24 late here Friday and a high of US$0.7573 last week.
Resistance was seen at US$0.7530 and US$0.7550, the latter proved decisive in defeating a week of rally attempts, while support was expected at US$0.7390 should US$0.7440 crack.

It tumbled to 83.63/73 yen on the crosses, its lowest close since August 1996, from 85.15/25 late here Friday. It followed the US$/yen which dove to 112.40/45 yen from an early 114.10/15 as a huge 129 percent rise in Japan's 20-day trade surplus for June stoked worries about trade tensions with the U.S.
In trade weighted terms the local currency sagged to 56.7 from 57.3 late Friday, a fall of over one percent.
Dealers said the impact of the gold price on the A$ tended to be overstated and the currency had a far closer correlation to base metals in recent years.
Nevertheless, the yellow metal is Australia's second largest export earner and the size of the fall would tend to depress influential indicators like the Commodity Research Bureau index.
This was particularly important at this moment in time since the index had plunged over seven percent since mid-May to breach major technical support at 236.00 last Thursday.
The close of 235.57 was its lowest since August 1995 and, if the break was sustained this week, analysts saw a risk of reaching 230.00 or even 220.00 in the medium to long term.

Among domestic features, a 0.5 percent rise in ANZ job advertisements for June was too marginal to have any impact. But it did serve to support suspicions the June employment data on Thursday would not be strong enough to curb speculation of another official interest rate cut. The data have been a useful leading indicator in the past, although recent volatility -- it leapt 16.7 in April only to fall 7.3 percent in May -- made it hard to detect the message amid the noise.

Median expectations for employment favour a rise of around 40,250 in June, which would almost exactly correct the 40,300 drop seen in May. It was that shock fall which first had the market scenting a fifth rate cut and it would take a much stronger gain this time to convice it otherwise.
"My line in the sand for jobs is 60,000," said J.P. Morgan senior economist John Kyriakopoulos. "That's the least it would take to make me reconsider the outlook for growth and rates."
His own forecast is for a rise of 30,000 in employment with unemployment stuck at 8.8 percent.
There was stronger news from data on motor vehicle sales.
New motor vehicle sales jumped 18.8 percent in June to 70,707, the best month on record, according to figures from the the Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries.

That strength saw the FCAI lift its 1997 sales forecast to 660,000, its highest in 10 years, from 640,000. In year-to-date terms sales of sports cars were up 41.7 percent and luxury cars 25.1 percent, growth which sat oddly with low readings in consumer confidence and subdued retail trade.
With autos accounting for a large chunk of retail sales, the data boded well for an upbeat sales report in June.
